terms.gloss: a height to look out from, a lookout
evidence: Varr. LL 6.82: Specula, dē quō prōspicimus
Verg. A. 3.239: dat signum speculā Mīsēnus ab altā
terms.comment: Varro’s definition is the thing itself: the place from which we look out. It is often a watchtower, and in speculīs esse is to be on the watch; for a viewpoint visited for the view, say what one sees from it (unde longē ac lātē prōspectus est, Livy). The e is short, as in speculum.

phrases.latin: Ascendāmus in illam speculam; inde tōtam urbem et flūmen vidēbimus.
phrases.english: Let’s go up to that viewpoint; from there we’ll see the whole city and the river.

phrases.latin: praegressus signa Hannibal in prōmunturiō quōdam, unde longē ac lātē prōspectus erat, cōnsistere jussīs mīlitibus Ītaliam ostentat
phrases.english: going on ahead of the standards to a spur with a wide view, Hannibal halted the soldiers and showed them Italy

sources: Lewis & Short: specula · Lewis & Short: apopsis · Lewis & Short: prospectus
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 9, s.v. belvedere.
